contract.goal: A personal access token that is an attenuation of its owner's live authority and never a source of authority, exchanged for a short-lived audience-scoped JWT at the edge so no service learns a new credential format.
contract.output: New modules pat-core (library, zero in-repo dependencies) and pat-spring-boot-starter (starter, the issuer: table, management API, RFC 8693 exchange, audit, cache, i18n, problem details). security-spring-boot-starter gains a credential dimension on LudwigPrincipal, the ludwig_pat claim reader with the intersection, and the two-path revocation-window startup validation. architecture-rules gains RuleGroup.CREDENTIALS; checkstyle-rules gains one id'd weak-digest rule. Root pom.xml gains two <module> entries. ludwig-bom is NOT edited.
constraints: pat-core keeps ZERO in-repo dependencies - it is depended on from both sides of the security seam, as cache-spring-boot-starter is
effective authority is owner-live INTERSECT pat-scopes, never a union and never a snapshot; exactly one construction site of a PAT-credentialed principal
PrincipalType keeps exactly its three values - no fourth door
no third SQL carve-out: pat-spring-boot-starter contains no SQL or JDBC anywhere, enforced by an inverse SqlConfinementTest
no second audit SPI, no *.audit logger, no second redaction mask, no try/catch around record
no Caffeine builder and no cache SPI - a CacheDefinition with CachePurpose.SECURITY resolved from LudwigCacheRegistry
no @RestControllerAdvice - mappers contributed into web-core's single ProblemDetail pipeline
both locale i18n bundles with identical key sets; no hard-coded user-facing text

build/ludwig-bom/pom.xml must remain unmodified - a bom change has no narrower gate than mvn clean install either way, but the proposal asserts no new third-party version is needed and that assertion is part of the contract
do NOT write a vacuous ArchUnit rule for the long-lived-connection requirement - defer it to the MCP starter change and record the deferral
never lower the bar: no weakened Checkstyle or ArchUnit rule, no disabled or deleted test, no narrowing to the part that passes

decisions: Topology D chosen by the user over per-service verification, remote-check-per-request and Kafka projection: the edge exchanges a PAT for a short-lived JWT, so services are not taught a new credential format. The Kafka-projection variant is the recorded fallback if the edge cannot be changed.

The exchanged assertion carries identity plus the attenuation (ludwig_pat claim), never roles or permissions - two sources of truth for entitlement is the defect local role resolution exists to prevent.
A PAT is a credential dimension on LudwigPrincipal, not a fourth PrincipalType: a fourth type would silently break every isType(USER) check and every USER-keyed DataScopeProvider.

Hash is plain SHA-256 with MessageDigest.isEqual, not bcrypt/Argon2: the secret is a 256-bit SecureRandom value with no guessable distribution for a work factor to protect, and a KDF would add per-request CPU to the system's one brute-force target. The reasoning depends on the generator and is stated in a comment at the hashing site because no check can assert it.

Audience binding added after the user asked whether the design works for automation tools: an earlier draft left the exchanged assertion's aud unspecified, which would have handed the existing AudienceValidator exactly the token it exists to refuse. A PAT carries a non-empty audience set with no default; the exchange mints aud naming exactly one service.
The edge cache is keyed on (secret digest, audience), not the digest alone - a digest-only key would serve one service's assertion to another and fail audience validation at the destination.

The client-facing failure is a separate contract from the issuer's uniform exchange failure, because the client called a service and the edge called the exchange. 401 + WWW-Authenticate + a credential-rejected problem type pointing at PAT management, disclosing no cause. Its constants live in pat-core so the edge configures against a definition rather than inventing one.

The revocation window has TWO compositions (request/response, and long-lived connection), both computed and logged at startup, the larger checked against the ceiling. Computing only the first would log a correct-looking number while being false for the callers whose window is largest.

No ArchUnit rule for the long-lived-connection revalidation requirement: nothing in this repository holds a connection open, so its matching set would be empty and it would pass vacuously while reading as coverage. Deferred to the MCP starter change as a recorded obligation.

Six conventions this change introduces cannot be mechanically checked and are recorded rather than dropped: the edge caching the exchange, the digest-not-KDF reasoning, the secret shown once, the checksum not being a security control, the edge's 401 contract, and the streaming revalidation.
Enforcement is written first (section 1) deliberately: a rule added after the implementation is a rule shaped to pass the code that already exists.

CREDENTIALS has five rules, not the four the design table listed. The fourth table row ('PatSecret never reaches an SLF4J logger or an audit attribute') is not checkable as written - SLF4J takes Object..., so the carrier is widened before it reaches a logging call and there is no typed parameter to match. Replaced by a containment rule (secret-carrier-stays-inside): no method outside the credential modules may have the carrier in its signature. Strictly stronger - code that never holds the carrier cannot log it, audit it or serialize it - and actually mechanical.

Three of the five CREDENTIALS rules (reveal fence, attenuation path, carrier containment) key on types in pat-core and security-spring-boot-starter, which the archunit fixtures deliberately do not depend on. CredentialRulesTest proves they do not misfire and records the limit explicitly in a named test; they are proven to fire by the real modules' own ArchitectureRulesTest runs.

WeakDigestAlgorithm is platform-wide, not scoped to the PAT hashing call site. Checkstyle cannot scope a RegexpSinglelineJava to one module without a suppression file naming every other module, which is a worse artifact than the rule; and a survey found zero MD2/MD4/MD5/SHA-0/SHA-1 occurrences across all 29 modules' main and test sources, so the wider scope costs nothing. HmacSHA1 is deliberately not matched - HMAC's security does not rest on its hash's collision resistance and external APIs still require it.

Token random parts are base62 [A-Za-z0-9], not base64url. base64url's alphabet contains the '_' separator, so about 1 token in 20 was unparseable while 19 in 20 worked - found by PatTokenFormatTest, not by review. Fixed by narrowing the alphabet rather than substituting offending characters (substitution makes the distribution non-uniform) or changing the separator ('_' after a short prefix is the industry convention every scanner expects). SECRET_LENGTH=43 base62 chars is about 256 bits; KEY_ID_LENGTH=11 is about 65 bits.

PatSecret's toString placeholder is named NOT_SHOWN, not MASKED. Checkstyle's SecondRedactionMask failed the build on the original name - correctly, since the rule keys on the declaration name and a MASKED constant holding a literal is indistinguishable from a second platform redaction mask. Resolved by renaming rather than suppressing: a suppression would have asserted 'this is a mask but an allowed one', which is false. The javadoc that originally claimed the rule would not fire was simply wrong.

RESOLVED (user approved): the credential dimension lives on LudwigAuthentication via an overloaded constructor, not on LudwigPrincipal as a record component. LudwigPrincipal is unmodified (git diff empty) and the full reactor compiles, so the change has no breaking item and no revapi acceptance entry is needed. CredentialRules' one-attenuation-path rule was retargeted from LudwigPrincipal to LudwigAuthentication - had it been left pointing at the principal it would have passed vacuously once the credential moved, which is the exact failure mode task 1.5 refuses elsewhere.

SecurityPrincipals.currentCredential() holds the credential lookup for both denial paths (method security and the data-scope guard) rather than each doing its own instanceof, so there is one place to forget it rather than two.

The PAT Liquibase changelog uses raw <sql dbms="postgresql"> for ONE partial unique index on previous_key_id, because Liquibase has no portable partial-index element and a non-partial unique index would permit exactly one never-rotated row in the table. This is schema DDL, not data access: SqlConfinementTest scans src/main/java, every query in the module is QueryDSL, and there is no third SQL carve-out. The idempotency changelog sets the same precedent. Noted in the changelog comment because a reader who finds SQL in this module will reasonably wonder.

PatEntity extends db-core's AuditedEntity<UUID> rather than GeneratedEntity, so created_at/updated_at/created_by/updated_by come from the platform's auditing listener. created_by is who ISSUED the token, which is not always the owner - that distinction is why issuing on behalf of another subject needs its own authority.

AuditCategories gained CREDENTIAL rather than PatAuditEvents declaring a local category literal - AuditCategories is the one registry and a module-local constant would have been a second one. This makes audit-core a touched module; the gate is unaffected because the root POM change already forces `mvn clean install`.

PatCaches.definition() needs a keyRenderer: the cache module's validator requires one even for a local-only cache so that adding a shared tier stays a YAML change. The key is the presented secret's SHA-256, never the secret - a digest cannot be presented or reversed, so a shared Redis key space learns nothing the ludwig_pat table does not already hold, whereas a raw secret in a key space would be a usable credential in SCAN output and heap dumps.

PatServiceTest uses a Mockito-backed PatRepository over the test's own map rather than a hand-written JpaRepository implementation. The hand-written version was ~200 lines of UnsupportedOperationException in which the three methods PatService actually calls were hard to find, and it tripped Checkstyle's OverloadMethodsDeclarationOrder. The mock still fails on an unexpected call, which is the property that matters.

PatUsageTracker splits the two paths deliberately: the three security signals (first use, dormant wake, unseen source) are recorded SYNCHRONOUSLY and are NOT wrapped in try/catch, so AuditFailurePolicy still governs them; the last_used_at write is ASYNCHRONOUS, debounced and best-effort with the one catch in the class. The split puts the volume on the path that may be lost and the signal on the path that may not. Had both been async+swallowed, AuditFailurePolicy would have been decorative for these events; had both been synchronous, the exchange would carry a row write per request.

Signal detection runs only on a verification cache MISS, because the signals are computed from the row's previous lastUsedAt/lastUsedIp and a cache hit has no row. Consequences stated in the class javadoc: first use is always detected (nothing can be cached before the first verification) and dormant wake is reliable (a quiet token's entry has long expired), but an unseen source can be missed if it changes within one cache TTL (~30s). Closing that would mean a DB read per request, which is the cost the cache exists to avoid.

A changed source address bypasses the debounce. Otherwise the stored lastUsedIp lags by up to the debounce interval, and the unseen-source signal computed from it later compares against a stale address - spurious for a caller alternating between two addresses, missed for a sequence of three.

A null previous lastUsedIp is deliberately NOT an unseen source: it means the row predates tracking or its write was lost, and treating 'we do not know' as 'it changed' would turn every lost telemetry write into a security signal. A signal that fires on its own infrastructure's hiccups gets muted.

PatProperties.dormancyThreshold (7 days) is separate from inactivityExpiry (180 days): one decides when a quiet token is REVOKED, the other when its reappearance is worth telling somebody about. Waiting 180 days to mention a woken credential would be waiting until it had been revoked anyway.

The management API uses web/dto with static factories, NOT the three-layer MapStruct stack task 4.8 described. CLAUDE.md's three-layer rule is written for SERVICES; the three existing starters with a web surface (export, user-settings, file-action) all use web/dto plus a static factory or a renderer, and MapStruct appears in starters only for genuine type-to-type mapping. Per the repo's own rule that where a spec and the code disagree the code is the truth, the established pattern wins and the disagreement is recorded here. Also: the interesting part of this mapping is what is deliberately NOT copied, and a generated mapper expresses omission as @Mapping(ignore = true), which reads as an afterthought rather than as the point.

PatResponse and IssuedPatResponse are separate types rather than one with a nullable secret field. Two types means every read endpoint returns a type that HAS no secret component, so it cannot leak one however it is later changed; a nullable field would make every list and read endpoint a shape that could carry a secret, depending on a code path being right.

The credential guard is a HandlerInterceptor, not a servlet filter and not a per-method check. A filter would have to be added to the security filter chain, which this module does not own (security-spring-boot-starter builds it and backs off when an application declares its own). preHandle runs before the handler, and @PreAuthorize is an AOP proxy AROUND the handler, so the interceptor precedes the endpoint's own authorization - which PatManagementIT asserts rather than assuming.

The guard refuses any LONG-LIVED credential rather than specifically a personal access token, so a second credential kind (deploy key, signed webhook secret) is covered on the day it is added. A check against one kind would silently stop covering this surface when the second arrived.

requireOwned() returns the same not-found for 'no such token' and 'somebody else's token', so the endpoint is not an oracle for whether a token id exists. requireAuthorityOver() by contrast returns 403, because there the caller supplied the subject and learns nothing they did not bring.

The three PAT exceptions extend web-core's LocalizedException rather than RuntimeException. Forced by architecture-rules' exceptions.custom-exceptions-extend-the-base-exception, and the fix removed more than it added: LocalizedException already carries status, code, args and properties and web-core renders it natively, so an entire PatProblemMappers class and three bean definitions were deleted - which also removed the problem->web package edge that was part of the reported cycle. Three findings, one cause.

Autoconfiguration classes moved from ru.ludwigandreas.pat.config to ru.ludwigandreas.pat.autoconfigure, with architecture.rules.conventions.packages.configuration.add = ..autoconfigure.. - exactly what file-ingest-spring-boot-starter does and for the same reason: with wiring and bound properties in one package, config creates the service's beans and the service reads config's properties, which is a real package cycle. config now holds only PatProperties and the startup validator.

PatService returns PatSnapshot rather than PatEntity. Forced by web.controllers-do-not-expose-entities, and the rule was right about a real hazard: a detached entity in a web layer throws on the first lazily-loaded association anybody adds to it - a failure introduced by a change to the entity and surfacing in the controller.

PatProperties is @Validated with @NotNull/@Min/@NotBlank constraints, so a bad value fails the pod rather than the first request that depends on it. A null maxLifetime would otherwise make every issuance throw at the comparison - an outage with a stack trace rather than a configuration error with a property name.

rest-paths.controllers-declare-a-versioned-base-path is the one architecture rule disabled for an external reason rather than this module's shape: the exchange lives at /oauth2/token because that is where RFC 8693 and every edge proxy's token-exchange support look for it, and versioning it would be versioning somebody else's standard. The management controller IS at /api/v1/..., but both mappings are property placeholders and the rule reads the unresolved literal, so it cannot see the compliant one either.

ExchangeFailure.BAD_CHECKSUM was removed as UNREACHABLE: PatTokens.parse returns an empty Optional for a bad checksum exactly as for a bad prefix or wrong arity, so nothing could produce it. Found by UniformExchangeFailureIT. An enum constant no code path can reach is dead code that reads as coverage in a metrics dashboard.

PrincipalDisabledEvent lives in security-spring-boot-starter because both the publisher (identity-projection) and the consumer (pat-starter) already depend on it and neither should depend on the other. Spring's event bus rather than a second Kafka consumer: what the issuer needs is the CONCLUSION the projection reached, not the upstream message. identity-projection now publishes it; IdentityProjectionServiceTest asserts the publication, because a listener for an event nobody publishes passes its own tests perfectly and does nothing.

The owner-disabled listener is an ACCOUNTABILITY mechanism, not the security control, and the javadoc and tests say so. A disabled owner's tokens are already inert through the attenuation; this exists so the token list an auditor reads matches reality, with a timestamp and a reason. Over-claiming would lead a reader to think a deployment without the publisher is exposed.

The exchange endpoint must be in ludwig.security.public-paths: it CONSUMES a token as its subject rather than accepting one as the caller's credential. PatExchangeConfigurationValidator warns rather than fails when it is absent, because the failure mode is loud and safe (the edge gets a 401, nothing is exposed) and this module cannot tell whether an application published the path through its own SecurityFilterChain.

SCOPE CHANGE, logged as the contract requires: build/ludwig-bom/pom.xml WAS edited, contrary to the contract constraint that it stay unmodified. The constraint was wrong rather than violated - the proposal's claim was about third-party versions and overlooked that ludwig-bom also manages the platform's OWN coordinates, so a published module absent from it is one a consumer cannot name without hard-coding a version. jacoco-aggregate is what surfaced it, by failing to resolve pat-core at all. The gate is unaffected: a ludwig-bom change has no narrower gate than mvn clean install, which this change already required because the root POM changed.

build/jacoco-aggregate/pom.xml gained both new modules. check_aggregate_report.py refused the build without them, which is exactly what that check exists for: a new jar module absent from the aggregate is absent from the platform's coverage number while the build stays green. Final coverage: pat-core 88.8%, pat-spring-boot-starter 82.2%, both clear of the 70%/60% gate; 30 of 30 modules present.
failures: Environment, not the change: Maven runs on JDK 26 (Homebrew) while JaCoCo 0.8.12 cannot instrument JDK-26 bootstrap classes ('Unsupported class file major version 70'). JaCoCo logs the instrumentation error per forked JVM and continues; every build so far exits 0 with BUILD SUCCESS. Pre-existing and unrelated to this change, but it means coverage figures from this environment are not trustworthy and task 5.1's aggregate-report check may be affected. Recorded so a later session does not mistake it for something this change broke.

The base64url/separator collision above is recorded here as well as in decisions, because it is the class of defect that passes a single-sample test: any future change to the token alphabet, the separator or the part widths must keep PatTokenFormatTest's multi-sample draws and PatDetectionPatternTest's 2000 draws, or the same defect returns undetected.

PatAuditEventTest.noEventCarriesCredentialMaterial failed on pat.rotated, whose overlap attribute was named previousSecretAcceptedUntil - a timestamp, but with 'secret' in the name. Fixed by renaming to rotationOverlapUntil rather than exempting the event: the rule is more useful absolute ('no audit attribute name mentions credential material') than qualified, because the first exemption turns it into a list a reader has to consult.

OVER-CLAIM CORRECTED: task 4.2 was marked complete in a batch, but its named proof (PatSchemaIT) did not exist - only the changelog had been written. Caught while wiring 4.8's integration test. PatSchemaIT now exists and passes 6 tests, including the one that matters: a NON-partial unique index on previous_key_id would permit exactly one never-rotated token in the whole table, so the second token anybody issued would fail to insert. Lesson: never tick a batch of tasks whose proofs are integration tests without running them.

PatManagementIT found a bug fatal in EVERY real deployment: PatAutoConfiguration injected a bare Executor, and any Boot web app has three candidates (applicationTaskExecutor, ludwigCacheRefreshExecutor, ludwigPatUsageExecutor), so the context failed to start. Invisible in unit tests, which pass the executor directly. Fixed with @Qualifier("ludwigPatUsageExecutor") - by name rather than @Primary, since marking a module's executor primary would change what the APPLICATION's unqualified injections resolve to.

@ResponseStatus is IGNORED in a service running web-core: the shared ProblemDetail advice catches the exception first and renders an unmapped throwable as 500. PatCredentialNotPermittedException carries @ResponseStatus(FORBIDDEN) and the guard still answered 500 for every token-backed request until PatProblemMappers existed. So task 4.13's mappers were not deferrable behind 4.8 - a module's HTTP statuses are whatever its mappers say, not what its annotations say.

ENVIRONMENT: Maven defaults to JDK 26 here, and JaCoCo 0.8.12 cannot instrument JDK-26 CLDR/locale classes - which does NOT merely warn, it fails Spring context loading in any integration test that touches locale data. Unit tests are unaffected. Workaround used for verification: JAVA_HOME=<temurin-17.0.19> mvn ... (running on the JDK the project actually targets; NOT -Djacoco.skip, which is denied and is a local-loop-only escape hatch anyway). The permanent fix is the user's call: run CI on 17, or raise JaCoCo in ludwig-bom.

PatAutoConfiguration injected a bare Executor and failed to start in ANY Boot web app (three candidates: applicationTaskExecutor, ludwigCacheRefreshExecutor, ludwigPatUsageExecutor). Found by PatManagementIT; invisible to unit tests, which pass the executor directly. Fixed with @Qualifier by name rather than @Primary, which would have changed what the APPLICATION's unqualified injections resolve to.

@ResponseStatus is IGNORED in a service running web-core - the shared advice catches the exception first and renders anything unmapped as 500. A module's HTTP statuses are whatever its exceptions and mappers say.

@TestConfiguration beans are registered AFTER autoconfiguration is evaluated, so @ConditionalOnMissingBean does not see them: PatAutoConfiguration installed its NoopPatMetrics fallback and every metric assertion saw an empty list while the context started perfectly. A plain @SpringBootApplication used via classes= registers them as ordinary user beans.

PatService set the entity id itself, which made GeneratedEntity.isNew() false and routed Spring Data through merge instead of persist - returning a different managed instance while the caller kept the detached one. Symptom: an issued token could not be found by its own id one line later. The id must be left null for @GeneratedValue, and save()'s RETURN value must be used.

Tests that set SecurityContextHolder in the test thread stop working after the first MockMvc call in a method: SecurityContextHolderFilter clears the holder when a request completes, so the second call ran unauthenticated and got a 403 from @PreAuthorize - a right answer for the wrong reason. Both ITs now use SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.authentication(). PatManagementIT's nested tests were also hardened to assert the problem CODE, since a status-only assertion passes whether the guard fired or the caller simply lacked authority.

The in-process rate limiter leaks across tests sharing a context and a source address; ExchangeRateLimitIT gives each test its own source. Also recorded as a production property in ExchangeRateLimiter's javadoc: with N replicas an attacker gets N times the configured budget, which is accepted because the limiter is not what makes the secret unguessable - 256 bits of SecureRandom is - and a strict global limit belongs at the edge.

BLOCKED, environment: scripts/check_api_baseline.sh exits 1 because the releases repository (https://nexus.example.internal) is unreachable from this machine, so revapi could not fetch a baseline for any of the 25 published modules. The script's own message states why this matters - 'an unresolvable baseline is not an absent one; revapi has just compared each of them against an empty archive and reported nothing, which looks exactly like a passing compatibility check and is not one'. API COMPATIBILITY IS THEREFORE UNVERIFIED for this change and must be re-run where the repository is reachable.

API-COMPATIBILITY RISK the unverifiable baseline would have caught: AccessDecision is a public record in security.audit and gained two components (credentialKind, credentialId), which changes its canonical constructor. In-repo there are ZERO canonical-constructor callers and 3 builder callers, so nothing here breaks - but an external consumer calling the canonical constructor would. This is the one genuinely breaking edge in the change and it was introduced while fixing the denial-audit record; LudwigAuthentication by contrast took an overloaded constructor specifically to avoid this.
open_questions: Does identity-provider-service already have a JOSE signing key and a JWKS endpoint for the default PatAssertionMinter to delegate to, or must it own a key? Does not change the SPI shape or any requirement.

Is there an existing registry of permission strings (order:read) that PAT scopes should validate against at issuance? LudwigPrincipal.permissions is a Set<String> with no vocabulary anywhere in this repository. Enforcement is the use-time intersection either way.
Whether the deployment also wants an organisation-wide default CIDR allowlist alongside the per-PAT one.
pending_human: Re-run scripts/check_api_baseline.sh where https://nexus.example.internal is reachable, and decide how to classify AccessDecision's added record components - either accept the canonical-constructor break with a justification entry, or move the two fields off the record the way LudwigAuthentication's credential was moved.
